clinicalPearls: A cumulative heavy-metal poisoning from ingestion or inhalation of lead, historically from paint, contaminated water, traditional remedies, batteries and occupational dust
Children are especially vulnerable, with neurodevelopmental harm at blood levels once thought safe; no threshold is considered entirely safe
Chronic exposure causes abdominal colic, constipation, anaemia, peripheral (motor) neuropathy and cognitive impairment
A blue line at the gingival margin (Burton line) and basophilic stippling of red cells are classic but insensitive signs
Encephalopathy with raised intracranial pressure is a life-threatening presentation, more common in young children
Diagnosis rests on a raised blood lead concentration; anaemia may be microcytic or normocytic
Management combines exposure removal with chelation therapy for significant toxicity, alongside public-health source control
reference.pathophysiology: Lead has no physiological role and disrupts multiple systems by binding sulfhydryl groups and displacing essential divalent cations such as calcium and zinc. It inhibits several enzymes of haem synthesis (including delta-aminolaevulinic acid dehydratase and ferrochelatase), causing anaemia with basophilic stippling and accumulation of haem precursors. Interference with calcium-dependent processes and mitochondrial function underlies its neurotoxicity, affecting the developing brain and peripheral motor nerves. Lead is stored long-term in bone, from which it can be remobilised during pregnancy or illness.
additionalDifferentials: Iron deficiency anaemia (may coexist and enhance lead absorption)
Other causes of abdominal pain (acute abdomen, porphyria)
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count and film (anaemia, basophilic stippling)
Abdominal radiograph if recent ingestion of lead-containing material
Radiographs of long bones in children (lead lines) where relevant
Assessment of renal function and neurodevelopment
redFlags: Encephalopathy: altered consciousness, seizures or signs of raised intracranial pressure
Wrist or foot drop indicating motor neuropathy
Ongoing high-level exposure, especially in a child or pregnancy
reference.prognosis: Prompt removal from exposure and chelation improve acute toxicity, but neurodevelopmental deficits in children may be irreversible; prevention and source control are paramount.
pitfalls: Assuming a safe threshold exists in children
Missing the diagnosis in vague abdominal pain, constipation and anaemia
Chelating without first removing the source (risking continued or increased absorption)
Overlooking traditional remedies, cosmetics or occupational hobbies as sources
